pedagogy.summary: Recognising that the faces of a 3-D shape are themselves 2-D shapes (a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid) is the bridge that connects the flat and solid worlds. It is best taught by taking solids apart — unfolding or 'popping up' a solid so its faces lie flat as recognisable 2-D shapes, tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. The key idea to build is that a solid is BUILT FROM 2-D faces, and that a face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.
bestPractices: Unfold or 'pop up' a solid from flat paper so children see the faces are 2-D shapes and can touch and count them (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Trace round, or dip-and-stamp, a face to print its 2-D shape — the print of a tin's end is a circle.
Name the face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) distinct from the solid's name (cylinder, pyramid, cube).
Contrast flat faces (rest flat on the table) with curved surfaces (roll), so a cylinder's curved side is not mistaken for a flat face.
Link explicitly: a cube is made of six squares; a cylinder has two circular faces — every 3-D shape is made up of 2-D shapes.
keyRepresentations: Pop-up / unfoldable solids whose faces flatten into 2-D shapes
Paint-stamp or trace-around prints of each face
A cube shown as six squares; a pyramid as triangles plus a square base; a cylinder as two circles plus a curved surface
commonMisconceptions: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'.
Cannot separate face from solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find (Mohamed & Kandeel 2023).
Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces (van Hiele visual level).

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn that the flat faces of a 3-D solid are themselves 2-D shapes — a circle on a cylinder, triangles on a pyramid. A solid with only flat faces, such as a cube or pyramid, is built FROM those flat faces; some solids, such as a cylinder, also have a curved surface, which is not a flat face. The core teaching moves are taking solids apart (unfolding or popping up a solid so faces lie flat), tracing or paint-stamping a face to print its 2-D shape, and handling solids to feel which surfaces are flat faces and which are curved. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether drawn on paper or sitting on the solid; the whole tin is a cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

activities.title: Take a solid apart into its flat faces
feedback: If a child names a face by the solid's name (calls a cylinder's end 'a cylinder'), trace round or stamp that face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is the 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder.
If a child calls a cube 'a square', pop up or unfold the six square faces so they see the solid is made OF squares, then help them re-name the solid.
If a child treats the solid as one undifferentiated whole, unfold it so each face lies flat and gets named, then rebuild it face by face.

Note for the teacher: a paper or card face has slight thickness and stands in for the ideal flat (zero-thickness) 2-D shape of the solid's face; ask the child what mathematical shape the flattened face represents, treating the paper as a stand-in rather than the mathematical shape itself.
activities.rationale: Physically constructing and taking apart solids lets children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, supporting them to distinguish and name component shapes; instruction is needed to move from seeing a shape as one whole to describing and composing its parts.
sourceClaims: Building solids from flat paper (pop-up) so children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, sides and vertices improved their ability to distinguish and name the shapes; children preferred 2-D shape names for solids until they physically constructed them, and the circle/sphere pair was the most secure.

At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
learnerActions: Handle a real solid (a tin/cylinder, a cube, a square-based pyramid) and run a finger over its surfaces.
Unfold or 'pop up' a solid made from flat paper/card so its faces lie flat, then touch and count the separated faces.

Name each flattened face by its 2-D shape (circle, triangle, square) and rebuild the solid face by face. If a paper cylinder is unrolled, its curved side flattens into a rectangle, but on the cylinder that part is the curved surface, not a flat face.
State the link aloud: 'a cube is made of six squares', 'a cylinder has two circular faces and a curved surface'.
activities.intendedInsight: A solid's flat faces are 2-D shapes; a solid with only flat faces (such as a cube or pyramid) is built from them, while a cylinder also has a curved surface. A face keeps its 2-D shape whether it is drawn on paper or sitting on the solid.

activities.title: Print the face: trace and paint-stamp
feedback: When the stamped circle appears beside the tin, confirm: 'the flat end is a circle; the whole tin is the cylinder'.
If a child tries to stamp the curved side, notice it cannot print a single flat shape — only flat faces rest flat and print cleanly.
Note for the teacher: the printed mark (and the paper it is on) has slight thickness; it represents the ideal flat 2-D shape of the solid's face, which is the shape the child names.
activities.rationale: Printing or tracing a face gives a child a 2-D artefact tied to the solid, which may reinforce that a face retains its 2-D shape off the solid as well as on it. This is a proposed activity; the cited study examined pop-up construction rather than stamping, so its efficacy here is unverified.
learnerActions: Dip the flat end of a tin in paint (or ink pad) and stamp it on paper; name the shape that appears.
Trace round a flat face of a cube or the square base of a pyramid and name the printed 2-D shape.
Set the printed 2-D shape beside the solid and say which face of the solid it came from.
activities.intendedInsight: The print of a solid's flat face is a plain 2-D shape (a tin's end prints a circle), making concrete that the face is itself a 2-D shape.

activities.title: Flat faces versus curved surfaces
feedback: If a child calls the cylinder's curved side a face, have them try to make it rest flat — it rolls, so it is a curved surface, not a flat face.
Confirm the cylinder has exactly two flat circular faces plus one curved surface.
activities.rationale: Explicitly contrasting flat faces with curved surfaces prevents miscounting the curved side of a cylinder as a flat face and sharpens the idea of a face as a flat 2-D shape. A sort can check how a child classifies surfaces but does not by itself elicit handling or an explanation, so it is paired with the resting-flat test.
learnerActions: Try to rest each surface of a cylinder flat on the table: the two ends sit flat, the curved side rolls.
Sort surfaces into 'flat faces' (rest flat) and 'curved surfaces' (roll).
Count and name the flat faces on a cube, a square-based pyramid, and the cylinder; note the cylinder's side is curved, not a flat face.
activities.intendedInsight: A flat face rests flat and has a 2-D shape; a curved surface rolls and is not a flat face — so a cylinder's curved side should not be counted as a flat face.

activities.title: Decompose every face (screen peel or physical net)
feedback: When a peeled or unfolded face matches the drawn 2-D shape, confirm they are the same shape shown in different places.
If a child forgets hidden faces, rotate the solid (or use the full net) to reveal them and count all faces before reassembling.
activities.rationale: Rotating a solid and separating each face addresses faces on all sides, including hidden ones, extending the decomposition idea beyond the faces a child can see at rest. A rotatable screen model is one optional way to show hidden faces; a physical unfoldable net works too — neither is uniquely required.
sourceClaims: At the van Hiele visual level shapes are viewed as a whole rather than by distinguishing their parts; instruction is needed to move children to describing shapes by their component parts and properties.
learnerActions: Rotate a solid, or its on-screen model, so faces on every side — including hidden ones — come into view.
On a screen model, peel each face off as a plain 2-D shape; with a physical solid, use an unfoldable net or pop-up so each face lies flat. Set each face beside a drawn version to compare.
Reassemble the solid from its faces and state how many of each 2-D shape it is made from.
activities.intendedInsight: Every flat face of a solid — not just the visible ones — is a 2-D shape, and a solid with only flat faces can be composed and decomposed from those flat shapes; a solid with a curved surface, such as a cylinder, also needs that curved part.

activities.title: Predict-then-stamp check
feedback: If a child predicts 'a cylinder' for the end's print, let the stamp reveal a circle, then discuss why the face is a circle while the whole tin is a cylinder.
A matching task confirms the outcome but not the take-apart reasoning — pair it with asking the child to explain how the solid is built from those faces.
activities.rationale: A predict-justify-observe routine makes the child's reasoning explicit before the stamp confirms or challenges it, which is more diagnostic than a match-only check.
learnerActions: Before stamping, predict and justify what shape the flat end of the tin will print.
Stamp it and compare the result with the prediction.
Match which 2-D shapes make up a given solid (e.g. two circles plus a curved surface for a cylinder) and explain the match.
activities.intendedInsight: Stating a prediction and reason in advance surfaces whether a child sees the face as a 2-D shape or conflates it with the whole solid.

constraints: Use real 3-D solids and named flat faces; ensure the solid itself is correctly named, because a child who calls a cube 'a square' has no distinct square faces to find.
Use a cube-shaped object when naming a cube, and a square-based pyramid when describing triangular faces plus a square base, so the named example matches the shape.

Paper or card cutouts, printed marks, and pop-up nets have slight thickness and approximate ideal zero-thickness mathematical faces; a flattened paper face represents the 2-D shape of the solid's face. Ask children what mathematical shape it represents, not whether the paper can be picked up, and state this approximation within the activity.
A screen model where a face peels off is an idealised representation; label it as a model and pair it with handling real solids so children also feel flat versus curved surfaces.
Matching 2-D shapes to solids checks the outcome only; it does not by itself show the child understands decomposition — combine it with constructing, unfolding, or explaining.

A fixed labelled image where tapping a face reveals its 2-D shape can serve as a reference, but it does not let the child physically separate and count faces; use it as a scaffold, not the main activity.

A sort or recognition/matching task may teach or check classification but does not itself elicit the child's own explanation of how a solid is built from faces; include tasks where the child names, counts, and reassembles.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. Activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The printing/tracing activity has no sourceClaims attached because the cited pop-up study examined building solids from flat paper, not stamping or tracing; its efficacy here is unverified.

The Common Core claim frames the overall objective (analysing 2-D/3-D shapes, describing parts, composing shapes) rather than directly evidencing any single activity's teaching move; it is retained as curriculum framing, not as efficacy evidence, and so is not attached to specific activities.

The original 'conversation' entry asserted that 'talk cannot carry the visual decomposition of a solid into faces'. This is a catalog comparison, not an established law; softened to: spoken explanation is useful to elicit a child's reasoning but is best paired with handling or constructing solids, since the decomposition is primarily visual and tactile.

The original claimed a rotatable 3-D model is 'ideal' and uniquely shows hidden faces ('the spatial crux'). The affordance (revealing faces on all sides) is retained, but comparative necessity over physical unfoldable solids is not established by the sources; both are offered.
The source efficacy claim (pop-up construction improved naming) comes from one kindergarten study; this micro-topic targets ages 6–7, so transfer is plausible but not directly verified.

assess.poeTask: Give the child a solid cylinder (a tin) and a stamp pad or paint. BEFORE stamping, ask them to predict and justify what shape the flat end will print. A child who thinks the tin 'is a cylinder' may predict 'a cylinder'; a child who sees the face predicts 'a circle'. Stamp it: a circle appears. The pre-stated reason is the diagnostic part — the print forces the idea that the solid's face is a 2-D circle.
probeDeeper: If I dip this flat face in paint and stamp it on the paper, what shape appears?
You called the whole tin a cylinder — but what shape is just this flat end?
How many flat faces can you find on the cube, and what shape is each one?
Is the curved side of the tin a flat face too? Can it rest flat on the table like the ends?
assess.correctAnswer: Identifies the flat round ends of the cylinder as circles and the faces of the pyramid as triangles (with a square base); explains that a face is the flat surface of the solid and is itself a 2-D shape, so the solid is built from 2-D faces — the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder, but each flat end is a circle.

errorPatterns.pattern: Names a face by the whole solid's name — calls the flat round end of a cylinder 'a cylinder' rather than 'a circle'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Trace round or stamp the face onto paper — the print is a circle; the face is a 2-D shape, the whole tin is the 3-D cylinder
errorPatterns.distractor: It is a cylinder (naming the face with the solid's name)
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Asked the shape of the flat face, gives the solid's name

errorPatterns.pattern: Cannot separate a face from the solid because the solid itself is mis-named — a cube called 'a square' has no distinct square faces to point to
errorPatterns.nextMove: Pop up or unfold the six square faces of a cube so the child sees the solid is made of squares and re-names the solid correctly
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Calls the cube 'a square' and cannot pick out its separate square faces

errorPatterns.pattern: Sees the solid as one undifferentiated whole and does not decompose it into faces at all
errorPatterns.nextMove: Unfold the solid so each face lies flat and is named; rebuild it face by face
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Treats the solid as a single object and cannot point out its separate faces

responseLevels.gap: Sees the solid as one whole and names its faces with the solid's name (a face of the cylinder is 'a cylinder').
responseLevels.full: Identifies each flat face by its 2-D shape and explains the solid is built from 2-D faces (a cylinder has two circular faces; a pyramid has triangular faces and a square base), distinguishing flat faces from curved surfaces.
responseLevels.partial: Points to faces and names familiar ones (the square faces of a cube) but inconsistently — misses faces on less familiar solids or denies a face is 'really' a 2-D shape.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Run your finger over this tin (a cylinder). Point to a flat face on it — what 2-D shape is that face? Now look at this pyramid: what shape are its faces? Tell me how a face can be a 2-D shape when it is part of a solid.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: A child who understands names the face by its 2-D shape (a circle) as distinct from the solid (a cylinder); a child who conflates them answers with the solid's name ('it's a cylinder') or denies the flat part is 'really' a circle because it is on a solid. The reason tier — how a face can be a 2-D shape — separates those who see the solid as built from flat shapes from those who see it as one whole object.

sources.claim: Building solids from flat paper (pop-up) so children hold, cut, fold and touch the faces, sides and vertices improved their ability to distinguish and name the shapes; children preferred 2-D shape names for solids until they physically constructed them, and the circle/sphere pair was the most secure.
sources.source: Mohamed & Kandeel (2023), 'Playful Learning: Teaching the Properties of Geometric Shapes through Pop-up Mechanisms for Kindergarten', IJEMST 11(1) (ERIC EJ1357339)

sources.claim: Kindergarten geometry asks children to analyse and compare 2-D and 3-D shapes and describe their parts using informal language, and to compose simple shapes to form larger shapes — framing the link between 2-D shapes and the solids built from them.
